Actually, buffering the entire point set directly with shapely gives me a union of circles around each point—if the buffer radius is large enough to capture connectivity, I get one smooth blob with rounded boundaries instead of the scalloped edges from raster morphology. That's cleaner and smoother than my pixel-based approach, so I should switch to that for the concave hull option.

Let me generate both the convex-buffer and this smooth points-buffer concave version side by side, then compare them against the bumpy raster version so the improvement is clear.

To make the points-buffer work properly, I need to calculate the right connectivity distance—essentially finding the maximum gap between fragments using their minimum spanning tree, then setting the buffer radius to half that value so the disks from neighboring fragments just touch and merge smoothly. So I'll set δ=2.0° to ensure connectivity, then write a script to load the data, compute the connectivity radius from the raster approach, and generate the improved two-panel figure using shapely buffers.

For the concave hull, I'll buffer the multipoint by δ and check if it produces a single polygon or multiple—if it's fragmented, I'll increase δ until it connects. NE="ne"; TGT="ESRI:54030"; fwd=Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326",TGT,always_xy=True)
LON0,LON1,LAT0,LAT1,RES=-180.,180.,-56.,84.,0.1

runame={countries.ADM0_A3.iloc[k]:countries.NAME_RU.iloc[k] for k in range(len(countries))}

pad=120; R0,R1=max(0,ys.min()-pad),min(ny,ys.max()+pad+1); C0,C1=max(0,xs.min()-pad),min(nx,xs.max()+pad+1)

    return np.array(g.exterior.coords)

размышление

I'm planning to visualize the world map with convex-buffer envelopes highlighting the top 20 most-fragmented countries. First I'll load the cached data from the lab, seedlab, and clist sources to avoid re-running simulations, then compute connected components for each country to count their fragments and rank them by fragmentation level. I need to be careful about archipelagos like the Philippines and Indonesia—their "fragments" are actual geographic islands rather than model artifacts, so I'll need to handle those cases appropriately.

The key challenge is distinguishing between model-induced fragmentation (where the model incorrectly splits a connected landmass) versus natural geographic fragmentation (real islands separated by water). I'm considering comparing each fragment against the actual country raster to see if it's reachable over land from the main body—if it is, that's model stranding; if it's on a separate island, that's natural geography. This approach would filter out archipelagos while capturing genuine model artifacts.

A simpler metric might be to calculate model-induced fragmentation as the difference between the number of components the model created versus the number of real geographic components for each country. This naturally downweights inherently fragmented countries and highlights where the model created extra pieces. t the real_components metric captures this well—model fragmentation minus actual country fragmentation. For Mongolia that's 21 extra pieces, Chad around 15, but Indonesia stays low since both model and reality have many islands. I'll rank countries by this difference and take the top 20 most fragmented ones. Then for each, I'm computing a convex hull around all the country's pixels and buffering it outward slightly to create an envelope that should contain everything while staying tight to the actual geography.

Now I'm rendering the full atlas map with these 20 envelopes overlaid on top. I need to decide on coloring—20 distinct colors would be ideal for clarity but hard to distinguish, so I'm leaning toward cycling through a set of distinguishable colors or using a single strong color with dark outlines for all envelopes.

Since these convex envelopes will likely overlap significantly across the map, I'll render them as outlines only (no fills) to avoid a cluttered appearance. The user wants to see how it looks, so I'll go ahead with thin-lined outlines in distinct colors cycling through a palette, each with a subtle dark casing to make them stand out against the atlas background.

For the final approach: I'll use the colored atlas as the base layer with thin borders, then overlay the 20 convex-buffer envelopes as bold outlines in distinct bright colors from a qualitative colormap. Since labeling individual envelopes on the map would be difficult, I'll add a legend showing all 20 countries paired with their corresponding envelope colors. I'll tint each country's territory in its assigned color with low opacity so the fragments connect visually to their envelope, then outline each envelope boldly in that same color—this creates a clear visual link between the scattered pieces and their container. The legend will complete the setup, making it easy to identify which envelope corresponds to which country. Computing the analysis script... Writing visualization script... Now I'll add the envelope outlines for each country separately, then verify that the containment is complete by checking the minimum coverage across all 20 countries—it should be 100%.

These oversized envelopes seem to be coming from countries with territories scattered far apart or those straddling the antimeridian, where the convex hull in longitude/latitude wraps incorrectly across the full width—Russia, the USA with Alaska, Fiji, Kiribati, and New Zealand are likely culprits, since their pixels span both near +180° and -180°, causing the hull to stretch the entire map width. The regional clusters themselves—Africa, Central Asia, the Balkans—are actually rendering reasonably well, so the visual noise is concentrated in just a few pathological cases rather than being widespread. Clipping the envelopes to the ±180 boundary or splitting countries by hemisphere would fix most of the problem. The giant envelopes are indeed from countries with real territory spanning vast distances—Russia, USA, France with overseas territories—so their convex hulls naturally become huge. Once I handle the antimeridian properly, the remaining regional overlaps should be quite workable. The real issue is that a handful of giant artifacts from antimeridian-crossing countries are making the visualization look worse than it actually is—the overlap statistics show it's mostly clean (max 5 overlaps, typically ≤2). I should show the user the image and give them an honest assessment: the core result works, but I can clean it up by filtering out those pathological cases so the ~155 regional envelopes display properly. Removing the >120° threshold helped, but there are still problematic envelope artifacts—an orange band stretching across the northern hemisphere that might be from Canada or another country with a large longitudinal span, and a pink horizontal band along the equator that could be from an antimeridian-crossing country like Kiribati or Fiji.

If a country truly crosses the antimeridian, its raw longitude span would be ~360°, which should've been filtered out. But maybe some of these remaining bands are from countries with spans just under 120° (so they weren't dropped) that happen to have pixels concentrated at extreme longitudes, creating the visual artifacts. I'm trying to figure out which specific countries are causing these bands and whether I need to adjust the filtering logic further.

Looking at the overall picture, even after dropping the worst offenders, there are still roughly 8-10 large countries (Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Indonesia, China, Kazakhstan, DRC, etc.) whose convex hulls sweep across huge areas and overlap significantly. The antimeridian crossers are the real visual problem. So empirically, the overlap situation is moderate statistically—most regions see ≤2 overlaps—but visually dominated by these large-extent countries creating busy, sweeping envelopes that make dense regions harder to read.

The key insight is that for big-extent countries, switching to concave hulls would be far more effective than convex ones. A concave hull hugs the actual territory shape and avoids the excessive foreign sweep that convex hulls create, especially for countries whose fragments are spread across their real geography. That's where concave geometry actually earns its value—not for scattered countries like Mongolia, but precisely for these large-extent nations where convex over-sweeps and creates clutter. — so I can show them both the cluttered full map and the cleaner version without the largest countries, then explain that concave hulls are actually the right tool for those big-extent nations since they'd hug the actual coastlines instead of sweeping over everything. I'll present both images with that verdict and offer to try a hybrid approach mixing convex for compact countries with concave for the sprawling ones.

The real issue is that the sea-fraction metric conflates two different problems: envelopes that bridge separate landmasses versus envelopes that naturally include some sea because the country has a complex coast. What I really need is to check whether the envelope connects fragments that sit on different landmasses—that's the precise test for whether it's actually crossing water.

For the antimeridian case though, Russia presents a wrinkle: even though Eurasia is technically one landmass, the cylindrical wrapping means Russia's Chukotka peninsula connects back to the rest of the country, so the landmass test alone wouldn't catch it. I'd still need to filter based on antimeridian span. So the solution is to combine both checks: skip countries with either multiple landmasses OR excessive antimeridian span. Implementing the landmass test with 8-connected component labeling on the global land mask, then checking each component for antimeridian wrap by detecting pixels spanning both the western and eastern edges of the longitude range — if both conditions exist, I skip that component since it indicates wrapping rather than a true landmass.

For components that pass the wrap test, I extract the unique landmass labels within each country's pixel set and skip if there are multiple landmasses (meaning the country crosses water between fragments), otherwise I draw the envelope. This catches overseas territories and island-spanning countries while preserving single-landmass countries even if their convex hull bulges into adjacent sea, since all fragments belong to one continuous landmass.

The approach is cleaner than using arbitrary sea-fraction thresholds. There's a potential edge case where a country with a tiny stranded island pixel gets skipped entirely because it technically spans two landmasses, but that's actually the correct behavior—the envelope would have to bridge over water to include that island, which is exactly what we're trying to avoid. Implementing the logic to skip envelopes that cross water or span multiple landmasses seems like the clearest approach — if the envelope would bridge sea, don't draw it at all. Computing the connected components of the land mask once, then checking each country envelope to see if it spans multiple landmasses or crosses the antimeridian—if either is true, skip it as a sea-bridge. This removes the sea-fraction rasterization step entirely, which is faster and more principled.

The user is asking whether they can build an interactive map with layer switching between a real map and a simulation, toggle borders at different administrative levels, click areas to identify countries, highlight entire countries or draw their boundaries, and potentially animate the simulation process. This is a substantial technical feasibility question about the overall architecture.

I'm thinking through how to answer this realistically by considering what data I have available from the Python pipeline—a 0.1° grid with 1.5M land cells, each labeled with a country and an admin center, plus arrival times from the coalescence simulation—and how to translate that into an interactive web experience. The key challenge is balancing data size with interactivity: I can render the base layers as compact PNG images for speed, but I'll need a separate ID raster (also PNG-encoded) to enable pixel-level lookups so clicking on the map can instantly tell you which country that cell belongs to.

For highlighting all cells of a selected country, I'll decode that ID raster into a typed array in memory and then iterate through it to find matching pixels—5 million iterations in JavaScript is fast enough, taking only tens of milliseconds. I'm also planning to precompute each country's envelope polygon as GeoJSON so I can draw borders and boundaries efficiently on the client side.

The projection strategy is to ship pre-rendered Robinson PNGs as base layers alongside an ID buffer aligned to the same pixel grid, keeping everything in fixed image coordinates. This avoids any reprojection math in the browser—clicks map directly to buffer pixels, and pan/zoom happen via CSS or canvas transforms. I'm also preparing two base PNGs (one for the real map, one for the simulation) that I can swap between.

For borders, I'll use separate toggleable PNG layers since they're simpler and lighter than vector for web delivery. Since borders differ between the real and simulated maps, I need four border PNGs total: national and internal borders for each version. When a user clicks, I'll look up the country ID in the buffer and fetch the country name from a JSON mapping.

For animating the simulation, the key is saving the arrival time (ctime) for each cell along with its country ID. Then in the browser, I can threshold the visualization at each time step to progressively reveal cells in the order they coalesced, coloring them by their assigned country.

The most efficient approach is to precompute a sorted list of cells ordered by arrival time, then incrementally paint only the newly-revealed cells each frame into an ImageData buffer. This keeps the animation smooth at 60fps without recalculating which cells to show every frame. The colors represent the country/seed that claimed each cell, so you see the coalescence process unfold as regions grow and merge.

The total payload is manageable—a few base and border PNGs, plus the arrival-time and ID buffers as images, along with JSON metadata for envelopes and names—coming to around 1-3 MB, which is easily deliverable as a single HTML page.

For delivery, I'm weighing single-file portability (inlining assets as base64, though that bloats the HTML) against a folder structure with separate asset files. Given the preference for self-contained projects, I could go either route, but a folder with index.html and assets alongside is probably the cleanest balance.

I also realize I don't have the arrival times saved from the original simulation—I'd need to re-run it with ctime and arrival data captured, which is about a 110-second computation but necessary to make the animation meaningful.

The user's asking whether this is all feasible, not necessarily asking me to build it immediately. I should give a straightforward yes, map out the architecture (how each feature connects to a specific technique), flag the one critical data export needed for animation, note the key constraints like the fixed Robinson projection space and incremental rendering, and then offer to start building—maybe proposing a phased approach. I'll answer the feasibility question directly and lay out the architecture, then propose starting the build with a choice about delivery format—single-file or folder structure. For resolution, 3600×1400 is workable but I can mention scaling down to 2400×930 if needed to reduce memory footprint. The id-buffer encoding using R and G channels can store up to 65,536 country IDs, which gives us plenty of room.

On click, I'll decode the PNG to an offscreen canvas once, extract pixel data, and look up the country ID from the R and G channels—ocean areas get a sentinel value like full alpha transparency so we know when there's no country. I'll keep a decoded Uint16Array in memory for fast lookups during highlighting. Admin-level regions would be a straightforward extension if needed later, but country-level handles the core requirements.

For envelopes, I'm shipping the 107 non-sea-crossing convex polygons as JSON arrays of pixel coordinates, then drawing them as polylines when a country is clicked—countries that cross the sea just get highlighted without an envelope outline. For the animation, I'm encoding arrival times as a 16-bit raster (either two 8-bit PNGs or a single PNG with time split across R and G channels), quantized to fit the full simulation duration, then each frame I increment a threshold to reveal which pixels have "arrived" by that time.

The challenge is that scanning all 1.5M cells per frame to find newly-revealed ones is expensive, so instead I'll precompute the reveal order once at load time by sorting cell indices by their arrival times—that's a one-time argsort of 1.5M values, which takes maybe 100-300ms and is acceptable. Then during animation I just stream through that pre-sorted list incrementally.

I'm thinking through the implementation: I could ship the time-raster PNG (compact) and do the argsort in JS at load, or use a counting sort on quantized time values for O(N) performance. Either way, the architecture is solid—fixed Robinson pixel space, base layers as PNG, an id-buffer PNG for picking and highlights, toggleable border layers, envelopes as JSON, and animation driven by the arrival-time raster with incremental reveal. The only new export I need is that arrival-time raster, which means a quick re-run of the simulation.

I should also weigh the tradeoffs: resolution granularity versus file size, and whether to inline everything in a single file or use an asset folder. Given the scope, I think the best move is to confirm the feasibility and outline a phased build plan, then offer to start.

Since the user works with single-file HTML, I'll note that base64-inlined assets are possible but will result in a 2–4 MB file, or we can use a separate asset folder. I'll propose building the static interactive version first—layers, borders, click-to-highlight, envelope visualization—which I can do immediately with the existing lab data, then add animation afterward once we re-export arrival times. That's a natural split and lets me begin right away.

Да, реализуемо целиком — каждый пункт ложится на понятную технику, и ничего экзотического не требуется. Ключевая идея: зафиксировать всё в одной системе пиксельных координат (та самая проекция Робинсона, в которой я рендерю), тогда в браузере не нужно никакой перепроекции — клики, подсветки и огибающие живут в координатах картинки.

Как раскладывается по фичам:

  • Слои «реальная / симуляция» — два готовых PNG-растра (раскрашенные карты), переключаются видимостью. Лёгкие, мгновенные.
  • Внешние/внутренние границы — отдельные прозрачные слои-оверлеи (свои для реальной и для симуляционной карты), включаются галочками. Можно растром (легче) или вектором (чётче на зуме, но тяжелее: ~35 тыс. нац. + ~73 тыс. внутр. сегментов).
  • Клик → какая страна — рядом с видимой картой кладётся скрытый «id-буфер»: PNG, где в каналах R,G закодирован номер страны (id = R·256+G, океан — спецзначение). По клику читаю пиксель → декодирую id → показываю имя (нужен маленький JSON id→название, в т.ч. по-русски). Тот же буфер один раз разворачиваю в Uint16Array — дальше всё быстро.
  • Подсветить все области страны — пробег по id-буферу (1.5 млн ячеек, ~20–40 мс) с заливкой совпадений на оверлей-канвас. Без задержек.
  • Огибающая — заранее считаю выпукло-буферные контуры (те самые, с отсевом «через море») и кладу как JSON массивов [x,y] в пиксельных координатах; по клику рисую линию. Для «морских» стран огибающей нет — будет просто подсветка.
  • Анимация симуляции — самое затратное, но тоже штатно. В симуляции у каждой ячейки есть время прихода фронта (ctime); экспортирую его отдельным растром (квантованным в 16 бит). В браузере — инкрементальный показ: ячейки сортируются по времени один раз на загрузке (counting sort по квантованному времени, O(N)), и каждый кадр дорисовывается лишь новая порция в ImageData. При длительности ~10 с это ~2–3 тыс. ячеек на кадр — идёт плавно. Визуально: фронты растут из админ-центров и сливаются в страны.

Что нужно доэкспортировать: для анимации — растр времён прихода (быстрый перезапуск симуляции с сохранением ctime, ~2 мин). Для статической части (слои, границы, клик, подсветка, огибающая) у меня уже всё есть в кэше — её можно собрать прямо сейчас.

Разумные развилки: разрешение растров (3600×1400 даёт чёткость, но можно ужать ради веса); и формат — единый самодостаточный HTML с ассетами в base64 (файл ~2–4 МБ) либо папка index.html + картинки/JSON (легче и быстрее грузится).

Предлагаю так: сначала соберу статическую интерактивную версию (два слоя, переключаемые границы, клик-инфо, подсветка страны, огибающая), а анимацию добавлю вторым шагом после до-экспорта времён. Делать единым HTML с инлайн-ассетами или папкой с файлами?

I'm planning to build an interactive HTML page with two map layers—one showing real data and another showing simulation results—that users can toggle between, along with clickable country detection, highlighting, and envelope drawing. Before diving into the code, I need to export the base data I'll need: raster PNG files of the coalescence map in Robinson projection space, plus the arrival time data for animations.

For the static version, I'll need colored map PNGs for both the simulation and real data, along with separate border overlays for national and internal boundaries on each layer. The real map's internal borders will represent admin-1 subdivisions (provinces), while the simulation map's internal borders will show the seed-cell boundaries from the coalescence process.

I also need two ID-buffer PNGs for click-picking—one for the simulation map and one for the real map—since the country assignments differ between them. Finally, I'll generate an envelopes JSON file containing the convex-hull outlines for each country on the simulation map, stored as pixel-coordinate polylines keyed by country ID.

For the remaining metadata, I'll create a countries JSON mapping IDs to country codes and names in both Russian and English, plus a meta JSON file with image dimensions, projection bounds, and palette information. The key technical challenge is ensuring a consistent pixel coordinate system across all these assets—I need to rasterize everything using the same affine transformation from Robinson projection coordinates to pixel space, so the id-buffers and envelopes align perfectly with the rendered images. Instead of trying to align separate renders, I should rasterize directly into a numpy array by working backwards: for each output pixel, use the inverse Robinson projection to find what (lon,lat) it represents, then look up the grid cell and its color/id at that location. This way everything stays perfectly aligned in the same coordinate space, and pyproj can handle the inverse transformation from projected coordinates back to geographic ones.

Building the output layers this way: create RGB images for both the simulated and real maps using the same union-based color palette so countries maintain consistent identity colors across both, generate id buffers encoding country identifiers in the red-green channels, mark ocean pixels as transparent, and compute national borders by detecting pixels where neighboring cells belong to different countries. Now I'm planning the export workflow: set the output dimensions (maybe 3600×H to keep it manageable) and figure out the Robinson projection extent by sampling the world boundary. I need to project a grid of coordinates across the valid latitude range to determine the actual x and y bounds in Robinson meters.

For the rendering, I'll iterate through each output pixel, inverse-project its center back to lon/lat, check if that point falls within the data bounds, and if so, sample the appropriate value. So for the real map, I need to rasterize the admin-1 polygon IDs to the grid to identify internal borders—where adjacent cells differ in admin-1 ID but share the same country. The user wants control over displaying both external and internal borders, so I should include both for the real layer. This is getting complex, but I'm thinking through whether to include it in v1 or simplify the scope first.

I'll rasterize the admin-1 geometries with their indices to create the real_adm layer, then use that alongside the country raster to detect borders. The admin-1 GeoJSON is large but I've loaded it before, so it should be cached. Once I have both rasters, I can build the output images by inverse-projecting each output pixel back to the source grid to resample the data.

For the inverse projection, I'm creating a meshgrid of output pixel centers and transforming them from Robinson to lon/lat coordinates using pyproj's vectorized operations—that should handle ~6.7M pixels in a second or two. Invalid pixels outside the Robinson boundary will map to NaN or out-of-range coordinates, which I'll mask as ocean. Then I'll use integer indexing to look up the corresponding grid values.

I'm settling on W=3200 pixels, which gives H≈1623 based on Robinson's aspect ratio of about 1.97. That's roughly 4.6M pixels total—manageable. Since the data only covers latitudes between -56 and 84, I'll crop the image extent to [-60, 85] to avoid wasting space on empty polar regions while keeping a small margin.

Now I'm projecting the lon[-180, 180] × lat[-60, 85] bounds using Robinson projection to determine the exact image extent, then saving out the PNG files: the simulated map with transparent ocean, the real map, and an ID map encoding region identifiers in the color channels.

I'm also generating separate border PNGs for national and internal boundaries in both simulated and real versions, with baked-in colors (dark for national, gray for internal) that the page can toggle. Finally, I'm converting the envelope polygons from geographic coordinates to image pixel coordinates and storing them in a JSON file keyed by country ID.

Now I need to build the metadata and JSON files—countries.json mapping IDs to country codes and names in Russian and English, plus meta.json with the image dimensions and palette info. Then the web interface will load these assets and layer them: a base map image that switches between simulated and real versions, toggleable border overlays, a canvas for drawing highlights on interaction, and an envelope overlay, with an offscreen canvas for the ID buffer to enable pixel-based country lookups.

My approach would be to scan the id-buffer for all pixels belonging to a given country, extract those coordinates, compute the convex hull using a standard algorithm like Andrew's monotone chain, then apply an outward buffer to match the style of the precomputed envelopes. The convex hull itself already contains all the country's pixels, so I could either add a margin by pushing vertices outward from the centroid or just use the hull directly since it visually encompasses the data. So when a user selects a country and enables the envelope feature, I'll compute the convex hull directly from the id-buffer pixels on the fly—this works universally for any country without needing precomputed data, and I can apply light rounding for a smoother appearance. This approach eliminates the dependency on the envelopes.json file entirely and makes the feature available for any country the user chooses.

I'll implement Andrew's monotone chain algorithm in JavaScript to compute the hull efficiently. For a selected country id, I'll scan through the id-buffer to collect all matching pixel coordinates, then run the convex hull algorithm on them—even for large countries with hundreds of thousands of pixels, the sorting and hull computation should complete in tens of milliseconds, which is acceptable. To optimize further, I could collect only the extreme points from each row (the leftmost and rightmost pixels of the country), which would reduce the point set significantly while still capturing the boundary.

Actually, that's the key insight: if I track the min and max x-coordinate for each row where the country appears, those per-row extremes are guaranteed to include all the convex hull vertices. For display, I'll offer the raw convex hull since it contains all pixels by definition, and I can optionally add an outward buffer if needed—but smoothing algorithms like Chaikin would cut inward and risk excluding pixels, which breaks the containment guarantee the user cares about.

For the buffer, instead of trying to offset edges (which is fiddly), I'll push each hull vertex outward from the centroid by a few pixels, then optionally apply Chaikin smoothing for rounding. This keeps things simple and robust while maintaining the containment property.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
import numpy as np, json, sys
from collections import defaultdict
import geopandas as gpd
from rasterio.features import rasterize
from rasterio.transform import from_bounds
from pyproj import Transformer
from PIL import Image
def log(*a): print(*a); sys.stdout.flush()
NE="ne"; TGT="ESRI:54030"; R=6371.0
fwd=Transformer.from_crs("EPSG:4326",TGT,always_xy=True); inv=Transformer.from_crs(TGT,"EPSG:4326",always_xy=True)
LON0,LON1,LAT0,LAT1,RES=-180.,180.,-56.,84.,0.1
nx=int(round((LON1-LON0)/RES)); ny=int(round((LAT1-LAT0)/RES))
tr=from_bounds(LON0,LAT0,LON1,LAT1,nx,ny)
countries=gpd.read_file(f"{NE}/ne_50m_admin_0_countries.geojson")
mask=rasterize(((g,1) for g in countries.geometry if g is not None),out_shape=(ny,nx),transform=tr,fill=0,dtype="uint8").astype(bool)
rr,cc=np.where(mask)
lab=np.load("coal_lab_01.npy"); ctime=np.load("coal_ctime_01.npy"); clist=json.load(open("coal_clist.json"))
cidx={c:i for i,c in enumerate(clist)}
runame={countries.ADM0_A3.iloc[k]:countries.NAME_RU.iloc[k] for k in range(len(countries))}
enname={countries.ADM0_A3.iloc[k]:(countries.NAME.iloc[k] if "NAME" in countries.columns else countries.ADM0_A3.iloc[k]) for k in range(len(countries))}
def to_grid(v,f=-1): g=np.full((ny,nx),f,np.float64) if v.dtype==float else np.full((ny,nx),f,np.int64); g[rr,cc]=v; return g
lab_g=to_grid(lab)
shapesC=[(g,cidx[a]+1) for g,a in zip(countries.geometry,countries.ADM0_A3) if (g is not None and a in cidx)]
RG=rasterize(shapesC,out_shape=(ny,nx),transform=tr,fill=0,dtype=np.int32).astype(np.int64)-1

# --- площади (cos-широты) ---
lats=LAT1-(np.arange(ny)+0.5)*RES
cell=(RES*np.pi/180)**2*R*R*np.cos(np.radians(lats))   # км^2 на ячейку в строке
cellgrid=np.repeat(cell[:,None],nx,axis=1)
def areas_by(grid):
    a=defaultdict(float)
    idx=np.where(grid>=0); vals=grid[idx]; w=cellgrid[idx]
    for c in np.unique(vals): a[int(c)]=float(w[vals==c].sum())
    return a
Areal=areas_by(RG); Amodel=areas_by(lab_g)
allids=sorted(set(Areal)|set(Amodel))
# --- индекс расхождения границ: симметр.разность / реальная площадь ---
diverg={}
for c in allids:
    rm=(RG==c); mm=(lab_g==c)
    inter=(rm&mm); only_r=rm&~mm; only_m=mm&~rm
    ar=cellgrid[rm].sum() if rm.any() else 0.0

The population-weighted cartogram model is working as expected—countries with large, dense populations like India, China, and the USA are expanding significantly, while sparse regions like Russia and Canada are shrinking. The rankings align with my earlier calculations, and Nigeria's divergence from typical patterns is interesting to note.

Now I'm redesigning the front-end to add the new features. I need to update the UI with additional panels for animation controls (play/pause, time slider, speed adjustment, and a live counter showing claimed territory), plus a new ratings section that can be toggled open.

I'll organize the layout with the sidebar handling layers, borders, click actions, and selected info, while putting animation controls in a bottom bar over the map for better visibility. The about and rankings panels will be modal overlays that open on button click to keep the sidebar clean.

For the app logic, I'm starting with a client-side envelope builder that scans the raster data for each country, finds the min/max x coordinates per row, constructs a convex hull using the monotone chain algorithm, then applies outward smoothing with Chaikin rounding to create the envelope polygon.

On country selection, I'll check if a precomputed envelope exists for that country in the current layer and use it if available (since those are nicely rounded and sea-filtered), otherwise build one client-side from the raster buffer. This gives flexibility to generate envelopes on demand for any country while preferring the polished precomputed versions when they exist.

For the info panel, I need to display the real area, model area, their difference, and divergence pulled from the countries data, formatting everything with thousands separators in square kilometers. The rankings modal will load two lists from the rankings file, and clicking an entry should select that country and potentially center the view on it.

For the animation sequence, I'm decoding the arrival simulation image to get quantized arrival times per pixel, then using a separate canvas overlay that progressively reveals the base map colors during playback—hiding the original base image while the animation canvas fills in, so the growth effect is visible, then swapping back to show the base map once the animation completes.

To handle the reveal order efficiently, I'm precomputing a sorted array of pixel indices using counting sort on the arrival values (0 to 65535), which gives me O(N + 65536) complexity. During playback, I maintain a position pointer that advances based on the current time, setting pixels in the animation canvas up to that point and tracking country-level counts. The slider maps directly to quantized time values, and I can find the corresponding pixel count either through binary search or by leveraging the fact that the order array is already sorted by arrival time. Implementing the reveal mechanism... Setting up the animation canvas as an ImageData object that I'll mutate each frame, copying base colors and setting alpha to 255 for revealed pixels. I'll layer the animation canvas on top of the base map, hiding the base and borders during playback to avoid mismatches with the final map state, then restore them when done.

I'm also adding a territory counter that displays either the selected country's progress (claimed/final km² with percentage) or the total land claimed percentage, updating it each frame and allowing the user to scrub through the animation while watching the counter change.

Now I'm writing out the full HTML structure with sidebar sections, buttons for about and rankings modals, the animation control bar at the bottom, and the canvas for rendering the map animation.

Writing the complete files... Completing the envelope lookup function...

I need to cache results per layer and ID, then implement the convex hull using monotone chain, expand by pushing vertices outward from the centroid, and smooth with Chaikin's algorithm. For the animation, I'm tracking the simulated area and pixel counts, then computing claimed area as the model area times the reveal ratio. The animation always displays sim coloring during playback, while the layer toggle controls the static view.

Now I'm starting to write the HTML file.

I'm writing the main app.js file that ties everything together—loading the metadata, country data, rankings, and envelope information, then decoding the various buffers for simulation IDs, real IDs, base colors for animation, and arrival data with build order tracking. I'll handle layer switching, borders, highlighting, and envelope rendering on the client side, set up the info panel to display area details, create modals for rankings and about information, build out the animation player, and wire up all the interaction handlers for panning, zooming, clicking, and hovering.

I need to be careful with how pixels are revealed during animation and manage visibility properly. I'm defining helper functions for convex hull calculation using the monotone chain algorithm, polygon expansion, and Chaikin smoothing, then writing out the full implementation.

For the animation system, I'm building data structures to track pixel arrival order—an arrival buffer marking when each pixel appears, a histogram counting pixels at each arrival time, a cumulative count array to determine positions, and an order array that stores pixels sorted by their arrival sequence so they can be revealed in the correct order during playback.

Building the reveal system with animation data, tracking how many pixels per country have been revealed, and implementing a revealTo function that either clears the animation state if rewinding or progressively copies base colors to the animation buffer while updating country reveal counts...

The play loop uses requestAnimationFrame to smoothly animate through the reveal sequence, maintaining a seek value that increments each frame based on playback speed, then converts that to a histogram bin index and calls revealTo to update the visual state and counter display, with the full animation timed to complete in about 12 seconds at normal speed.

For the UI controls, the slider lets users manually seek through the animation by pausing playback and jumping to a specific point, while the play button toggles between playing and paused states, resetting to the beginning if playback starts from the end. The visibility logic shows the animation view when the player is active (either playing or when the user has seeked forward), hiding the base map and overlays during this time.

I'm thinking through how to manage the transition between static and animated views—when the slider returns to zero and playback isn't running, the static view should reappear. Clicking should remain functional throughout both views since the ID buffer tracks positions independently of what's displayed. During animation, the highlight overlay can stay hidden to avoid clutter, but the live counter can still update when a country is selected. I'll create a setView() function to handle these state transitions cleanly.

Now I need to tackle decoding the base color data from the map simulation for the animation...

I'm also thinking through the reveal logic with seeds — at seek=0 the animation should be hidden and show the static view, but once playback starts the seeds appear first since they have arrival time 0. That's consistent.

I should write out the Russian description for the about section explaining the model clearly, then move into the full app.js implementation.

I'll cache the computed envelopes client-side to avoid recalculating them. For the convex hull, I'm implementing the monotone chain algorithm that sorts points by x-coordinate, then builds the lower and upper hulls by removing points that make clockwise turns.

I'm also writing a function to expand a polygon outward by a given distance, calculating the centroid first, then scaling each point away from the center.

Now I'm implementing Chaikin's algorithm to smooth a polygon through iterative subdivision, where each edge gets split into two points positioned at quarter and three-quarter intervals.

Writing envelope function... Caching the polygon and moving on to test the full app.js file with Node's syntax checker.

So the border imposedness index is actually a metric calculated per border pair between adjacent countries, not per country. It measures how much the real border deviates from where a spherical Voronoi reconstruction based on admin-1 population centers would naturally place it, then normalizes that deviation by the local population scale.

The local scale is the population-weighted mean distance from each border point to its 8 nearest populated places, which accounts for whether the deviation occurs across densely populated land versus sparse desert. The top-ranked borders like USA-Canada show high imposedness because they're straight lines cutting through populated areas far from where natural population-based divisions would fall.

The user wants to recalculate this using the population-weighted coalescence simulation instead of the pure geometric Voronoi, so rather than using equal-weight Voronoi edges as the baseline for "natural" borders, I'd use the simulated population-weighted version to see which real borders deviate most from that model.

The tricky part is that in the simulation, the border between two countries might not exist where the real border is—the simulation could assign that entire region to a third country. So I need to handle cases where the real border doesn't align with the simulation's territorial assignments, which is more complex than the Voronoi approach where every edge between two countries is guaranteed to exist. The key insight is to build a KDTree from all the simulation's inter-country border pixels (where the country label changes), then measure how far the real border points are from this simulated border tree. This directly mirrors the original approach but swaps the Voronoi diagram for the actual simulation boundaries. I can reuse almost the entire original script, just replacing the Voronoi tree construction with one built from the simulation's border pixels, then compute deviation as the mean distance from real border points to their nearest simulated border point, normalized by local scale.

Extracting the border pixels from the simulation grid... per-pair ranking as a list in the webmap's rankings modal, showing the most imposed borders. I could add a third tab for this or integrate it into the existing structure.

My approach: adapt the border ranking script to use simulation borders instead of Voronoi, then output the results as a JSON list of top border pairs with their imposedness metrics. This gets added as a new ranking tab in the webmap alongside the existing per-country divergence. The user's original concept of "несправедливость" maps directly to this per-pair imposedness, so featuring it prominently makes sense.

First I need to verify the populated places geojson file is available in the ne/ folder since the original script depends on it. Then I'll write a puppeteer test script to load and screenshot the current page while capturing any console errors—this will help me spot bugs before moving forward. After that, I can tackle the territory-difference layer, which will show per-pixel gains and losses by comparing the simulated country assignment against reality.

For the visualization itself, I'm weighing two approaches: either color each changed pixel by whether its sim-country gained or lost territory overall, or create a choropleth that colors entire countries by their net territorial delta with intensity reflecting magnitude. The choropleth approach seems cleaner and more intuitive for showing which countries gained versus lost.

I'll go with the diverging choropleth — rendering each country in the sim territory with a color mapped to its delta value on a red-to-green scale. This becomes a new layer option alongside the existing maps. I need to compute the delta per country, apply the diverging colormap, and render it as a PNG. I'll also need to set up the layer radio button and handle the ID buffer for interactivity.

For the legend, I can add a small scale indicator in the UI when this layer is selected. The diff layer will reuse the same ID buffer as the sim layer for picking.

Now I'm planning the implementation sequence: first, I'll test the current page with puppeteer to catch any bugs before adding more features. Then I'll recompute the imposedness metric using the sim borders and prepare that data for the webmap. I'm noticing that East Timor in the simulation got absorbed into Indonesia, which creates a huge deviation metric since the real border is nowhere near the simulated border—this is a degenerate case where the model essentially erased East Timor's existence, leaving its actual boundary with no corresponding simulated counterpart to compare against.

The US–Canada border at 2.82 still stands out as the clearest signal of an imposed boundary, with the 49th parallel being the textbook example of a straight-line colonial border disconnected from natural population patterns. Looking at the other high-deviation borders like Uganda–DRC, Mozambique–Malawi, and Russia–China, these all represent sensible cases of imposed colonial or political lines cutting through populated regions, which is what I'd expect to see flagged as genuinely "imposed" rather than degenerate artifacts.

The East Timor case is clearly problematic—a deviation of 1628km with the country essentially vanishing in the simulation means there's no actual simulated border nearby to measure against, making it a measurement artifact rather than a real signal. I should filter these out by excluding pairs where the deviation is implausibly large (say, over 700km) or where one country's modeled area drops below a meaningful threshold, since that indicates the country was absorbed and the measurement is meaningless.

The original Voronoi approach didn't have this issue because it always generated edges between adjacent administrative centers, but the simulation can completely absorb a country, leaving no border to measure. I'll rebuild the imposedness JSON with a simple filter applied during export—just reading the CSV and excluding pairs where dev_km exceeds 700, which removes the degenerate cases while keeping legitimate comparisons like US-Canada (382km).

Навязанность vs симуляции осмысленна: США–Канада 2.82 (архетипичная имперская прямая), Уганда–ДРК, Россия–Китай, Турция–Греция, Вьетнам–Китай. Но топ занял Восточный Тимор–Индонезия (dev=1628 км) — это вырожденный случай: модель поглотила Тимор Индонезией, поэтому рядом нет «модельной» границы. Looking at the territory-difference choropleth, the color coding makes sense for most regions—deep green for countries that gained the most territory like India, China, and the USA, and deep red for those that lost significantly. But there's something odd with Canada's coloring; it shows as green despite losing population, which suggests the visualization might be treating the USA-Canada region as a single entity where the USA's territorial gains are dominating the display.

Actually, I think I'm seeing how this works now. The map colors each pixel based on the SIM owner's net change—so land that became USA territory shows green because the USA gained overall, while the red fragments scattered across northern Canada represent Canada's remaining isolated territories, which appear red because Canada's delta is negative. Similarly, the deep red in Russia reflects its massive territorial loss, while the green sweep across Siberia shows where China and India expanded into former Russian and Kazakh land. The visualization is essentially showing which countries benefited from the territorial redistribution and which ones got carved up.

At 34% of the animation timeline, the visualization shows 98% of land claimed, with only tiny slivers of unclaimed territory remaining in the far north—places like northern Canada and Greenland appear as dark gray against the black ocean, since most populated landmass gets claimed quickly while sparse interior regions take longer.

The issue is that using linear time mapping creates a visually awkward animation: almost everything fills in during the first third, then the remaining two-thirds of the animation just slowly fills in the sparse bits, making it look frozen for most of the duration. A better approach would be to map by rank instead—revealing an equal number of pixels per frame—so the growth appears smooth and continuous throughout.

There's a tradeoff here: the physical-time animation is truthful to the actual data (sparse interiors really do take longer), but it's not visually satisfying. If I switch to rank-based revealing, the animation becomes smooth and the counter still shows the percentage claimed, which is what matters for UX. The slider would then directly control the fraction of pixels revealed rather than mapping through physical time, making the interface more intuitive. Updating the seek function to map the slider value directly to a fraction of total land, then calculating the reveal target and percentage label from that. This keeps the animation smooth and makes the land counter redundant with the time label, but the per-country breakdown is what matters. Let me implement this change and test it again — though I'm wondering if the visual skew I noticed earlier was just a quantization artifact. Switching to rank-based mapping removes the cumInc dependency (I'll leave it built but unused), and the counter's else branch already shows the right percentage, so that stays as is. Let me implement this and test it at 34%.

That's substantial, so I should prioritize strategically rather than trying to tackle everything at once, though the user did ask for all of it.

Let me organize by complexity and impact: the coastline during animation is the simplest and was explicitly requested, so that's the natural starting point. I need to figure out how the coastline is currently rendered—whether it's baked into the base map PNGs or drawn separately—so I can make it visible when the base layer is hidden during animation playback. I'm weighing whether to use a single coastline color that works on both the dark animation background and the colored static map, or create separate assets for each context. A medium gray around #707880 at 1px thickness could work across both — subtle enough on the colored land but visible enough against the dark animation backdrop.

Since the user specifically requested the coastline during animation, I'll add it as a persistent layer that shows always. The gray silhouette I'm already drawing during animation provides the land fill, but adding a crisp coastline line on top will make the land boundaries much clearer.

Now I'm prioritizing what to tackle: the coastline is a must-do (explicit request and quick to implement), while the other improvements like the gradient legend and ownership highlighting can follow. I need to export segment geometry as GeoJSON-like data in image coordinates so I can draw colored segments on the map. For animation polish, I'm considering front glow (computing the edge of the revealed region each frame), multiple counters in the UI, and PNG export via canvas. Given the scope, I'm prioritizing coastline rendering, adding a gradient legend with numbers and a toggle for changed owners in the diff layer, and implementing PNG export for the current frame.

Now I'm thinking through what's most valuable to tackle: drawing the imposed border segments colored by index as an overlay with a toggle to switch between Voronoi and simulation references. This is the most substantial feature, but it's also the biggest lift. I need to compute imposedness segments for both reference versions and export them, then wire up the toggle. Rather than try to do everything at once, I should focus on a coherent batch—coastline in the animation, the imposedness overlay with reference toggle, and the diff layer numbers—test it thoroughly, then iterate. Refining the scope: I'll handle the imposedness overlay with both sim and Voronoi reference toggles as the main feature, add the diff legend numbers and owner-change toggle, then layer in animation with coastline and PNG export plus front glow. The "only changed owner" filter can be computed client-side from the loaded ID buffers, so no separate export needed. For the Python side, I'm exporting the coastline as a PNG, then computing imposedness segments for both reference types—mapping each segment from geographic coordinates to image pixels with normalized indices.

For the Voronoi reference, I need to recalculate deviation from the spherical Voronoi geometry per segment rather than per pair. I'll sample points along each real border, compute deviation to the appropriate edge tree (Voronoi for the reference case, sim borders for the other), normalize by scale, and emit polyline segments with per-point norm values so the frontend can color each segment by averaging its endpoint norms.

I'm planning to export each border as a list of [x, y, norm] points in image coordinates, which the JS visualization can then color using a turbo colormap. This means building both the sim border tree and reconstructing the Voronoi tree from the original spherical Voronoi computation, then iterating through adjacent country pairs to sample their real borders and compute both norm values.

Writing export_borders.py... I'll sample the coastline points more sparsely at 0.2-0.3° intervals to reduce the dataset size. The export process will run in the background since it involves computing Voronoi diagrams and per-pair norms, which could take a minute or two. My plan is to parallelize this: start the Python export script generating the coast.png and imp_lines.json files, then simultaneously work on the front-end to add the coastline animation toggle, the imposedness overlay with reference toggle, update the legend, and implement the changed-owner filter and animation PNG export with glow effects.

For the coast.png generation, I'm extracting the coastline from the image-space land mask by identifying pixels where land borders ocean—essentially finding edges in the mask where a land pixel has at least one non-land neighbor. I'll sample the land mask through inverse projection to get per-pixel land classification, then draw a thin 1-2px line along those boundaries.

For the color, I'm settling on a neutral light gray around #9aa3b0 with ~0.85 alpha at 1px width—light enough to show continents clearly against the dark animation background and distinct from the darker national borders that sit inside the landmass.

I'm thinking the coastline should always be visible as a base layer beneath the internal borders, rather than toggling it on and off. It'll frame the continents subtly in the static view and naturally appear during animation, keeping the design consistent and simple. I'll add a separate canvas for the imposedness lines that toggles with a checkbox, and structure the UI with a new sidebar section for "Навязанность границ" that includes options to show/hide the layer and select between Voronoi or model reference. I'm also planning to add a checkbox for the diff layer to filter only changed boundaries, along with legend numbers.

Given the complexity, I'm going to split this into two phases: first I'll export the coastline and imposedness data from Python, then build out the UI components while that runs in the background. This way I can test the coastline animation, PNG export, glow effects, and the diff legend numbers before tackling the more complex imposedness visualization.

Let me start the export_borders.py script now, which will reconstruct the Voronoi diagram from the admin centers, compute the spherical regions and inter-country edges, then sample points along shared borders to calculate distance metrics.

def xyzll(p): return (np.degrees(np.arctan2(p[...,1],p[...,0])),np.degrees(np.arcsin(np.clip(p[...,2],-1,1))))

The export completed successfully with the coastline image and Voronoi data ready, plus the imposedness segments file. Now I'm planning the frontend implementation—I'll make all the DOM and styling changes in one comprehensive update, then validate everything with puppeteer. I need to add the coastline as a persistent image layer, create a canvas overlay for the imposedness visualization on the map, and integrate these with the existing animation and border elements.

For the DOM structure, I'm positioning the coastline image between the animation layer and the national borders so it stays visible throughout but doesn't obscure the borders. The imposedness canvas will sit above the overlay to display the colored segments, and I'm working through the exact layering to ensure everything renders in the right order.

Now I'm setting up the UI controls — a checkbox to toggle the imposedness display and radio buttons to switch between the model and Voronoi reference. The core drawing function will iterate through the imposedness lines, coloring each segment based on its normalized value using a gradient colormap that transitions from blue through green and yellow to red for higher values, with a cap around 2.5. I'm also planning a small legend to show what the colors represent.

Implementing the color mapping function... For rendering, I'll draw each line with a dark base polyline first for contrast, then layer the colored segments on top—that way the imposed/organic distinction stays visible even on the colored map. With 339 lines and a few thousand segments total, this approach is efficient enough. I also need to update the diff legend to display the actual magnitude numbers, showing something like "−11.7 / +10.3 км²" using the max diff value from the metadata. потеряли ← → приобрели (±${diffMaxM} млн км²)`.

Now I'm thinking about adding a toggle for "Только сменившие владельца" (changed owner) that highlights pixels where the simulated and real ownership differ. I could draw this as a semi-transparent overlay on a dedicated canvas to make changed areas stand out against unchanged land, or I could reuse an existing canvas for diff-related effects.

To keep things manageable, I'll use two separate canvases: one for imposedness lines and another for the changed-owner mask. When the toggle is active on the diff layer, I can overlay a translucent dark layer over unchanged pixels so the changed pixels show through with their diff colors.

For the implementation, I'm creating a function that iterates through each land pixel and checks if the simulated and real values match—if they do, it applies a dark translucent overlay; otherwise it stays transparent. This dims the unchanged areas and highlights what's actually changed. Then I'll add an export function that composites all visible layers together and downloads the result as a PNG.

Now I'm thinking about the animation's leading edge—I need to detect the frontier where newly revealed pixels border unrevealed land, so I can apply a glow effect there during playback.

The challenge is that computing this frontier every frame across the whole image is expensive. A simpler approach: just brighten the pixels revealed in the current frame for one frame, letting them fade back to normal the next frame—that creates a sparkle effect at the leading edge. I'd track which pixels were revealed this frame and draw them with a white boost on a separate glow pass, though putImageData overwrites complicate things.

A lightweight solution is to boost the brightness of newly-revealed pixels directly in the animation data itself, then restore them to their true color next frame by re-reading from the base color for those pixels. I'll keep an array of the pixel indices revealed in the previous frame and use that to manage the glow decay. Implementing the glow effect... I'm realizing there's a subtle issue with how the boosted pixels persist across different playback states. When the animation is paused or scrubbed, the last batch stays glowing on the canvas, which is mostly fine since the animation gets hidden when playback stops and the static base image shows instead. But if the user scrubs while paused, that glowing effect lingers until the next batch is revealed, creating a minor visual artifact that I need to think through more carefully. Now I'm planning out the implementation changes systematically—adding the coast and canvas elements to the HTML, creating a new sidebar section for the difference layer controls including the owner-change filter, inserting a PNG export button in the player bar, and updating the diff legend to show numbers. Then I'll need to update the app.js logic to handle loading and processing these new features. drawChanged needs to trigger on both toggle and layer change, while drawImp only needs the toggle since it's layer-independent. I'm going to write a comprehensive patch script to handle this carefully—given the complexity, I'll add the new canvas elements and UI controls to index.html, then patch app.js with the drawing functions and event bindings. Let me start by verifying the export files exist and checking the imp_lines.json size, then write out the front-end additions step by step.

I need to reorder the #world canvas and image layers carefully: base image, animation canvas, coast border image, then the two border images, followed by the changed-mask canvas (below the highlight), the overlay canvas for highlighting, and finally the imposedness canvas on top.

Structuring the canvas layers...

Now I'm adding a new sidebar section for imposedness settings with a checkbox to toggle the imposedness lines and radio buttons to choose between the model or Voronoi diagram as the reference.

I need to add a checkbox in the Layer section for filtering only properties that changed ownership, place it after the diff radio button, then add an export button to the player that saves the current frame as PNG. I'll also add a span to the difflegend to display the count.

For the app.js changes, I'm going to write a comprehensive Python patch to handle all the modifications carefully, making sure the string matches are exact. Starting with the setView function which currently controls the visibility of animation and base layers.

I'm refining the visibility logic for several elements: coast should always be visible and set once during initialization, impc (imposedness lines) should hide during animation for a cleaner look like the overlay, and fx (changed properties) should only show during static diff view so it hides during animation too. The overlay and impc will follow the same pattern.

Now I'm working on the impColor function... Finishing the line drawing with colored segments based on reference values, then moving on to set up the canvas clearing for the changed visualization...

Now I'm implementing the diff layer display, which compares simulated versus real values and marks matching pixels with a dark color and partial transparency. Then I'm binding UI event listeners to toggle the importance layer and other display options.

I need to set up the initial options object with flags for importance display, reference type, and change detection, plus load the importance lines data and configure the canvas elements for the coast and importance layers during initialization.

For the PNG export, I'm creating a temporary canvas and compositing all the visible layers onto it—checking which animation or base layer is active, then drawing the coast overlay and any enabled data layers before exporting.

I need to add a lastBatch global variable for the glow reveal function, and in setView I should manage the display states for the coast, impact canvas, and effects layer based on whether animation is active. Actually, the coast layer should probably stay visible by default, so I'll set that in initialization rather than toggling it in setView.

For the drawing functions, I should call drawImp() and drawChanged() initially after loading and whenever the layer changes. The layer change handler will need to trigger drawChanged() since the changed pixels depend on which layer is active, while the impact canvas content persists independently. I'll also need to make sure drawChanged() gets called in the layer radio handler after setLayerImages and redraw are executed.

Now I'm working through the glow boost logic—when it's active, it makes the lastBatch pixels bright, and when animation stops at the end, animActive becomes false and I need to handle the cleanup.

There's an issue with revealTo restoring lastBatch from baseColor; I need to make sure that when seeking backward, clearAnim properly resets lastBatch to an empty array.

I'm writing the Python patch script now, then I'll reduce the glow intensity to 0.5 to prevent washing out the image. After patching, I'll run the node check and then test with puppeteer to verify the coastline shows in animation, the imposedness lines toggle correctly, the reference toggle works, and the changed-owner diff displays properly.

I also need to verify the export button doesn't throw errors, then write both the index.html and app.js patches in a single Python script.

Let me think through this—if those pixels are Russia in both versions, the dimming logic should apply, but they're showing as bright instead. I need to reconsider whether the diff layer is actually coloring by the simulation owner's delta, or if there's something else going on with how the unchanged-owner pixels are being filtered. The bright green across North America likely reflects the territorial changes in the simulation—where the USA expanded into former Canadian land, those areas show as changed owners and remain bright, while unchanged USA territory should appear dimmed but is hard to distinguish at this zoom level. The dimmed olive regions are countries with minimal changes, so the visualization seems to be working correctly, though the contrast between dimmed and bright saturated colors is subtle. I'm still puzzling through why Russia appears bright red if it retained its core territory unchanged. Adjusting the visualization approach...

Instead of darkening unchanged pixels, I'll paint them as solid gray so the changed regions with their color differences stand out more clearly. This means setting unchanged areas to an opaque gray while letting the colored diff show through for changed pixels, making the distinction much sharper.

I'll set the colored line to 3.0 and the casing to 5.0 for a solid dark halo effect.

The user is asking about four substantive questions, and I'm starting with the first one about animation correctness. They're observing that when one country's territory expands in the simulation, it seems to pass through another country's region rather than flowing around it, and they want to know if this is a resolution issue or an actual problem with the model. I need to think through how the coalescence model works—specifically, that expanding fronts should stop when they meet each other, forming borders where territories touch.

In the animation replay, pixels appear based on their arrival times and are colored by their final owner. So if country A's territory wraps around country B, you'd see A's pixels appear on both sides of B during the animation, which could create the visual illusion of passing through. But the actual mechanism is that fronts propagate across the pixel graph and stop at contact points with other countries' fronts, then continue flowing around the obstacle. The question is whether there's a subtle edge case in how same-country fronts merge versus how different-country fronts interact that might allow one to pass through the other. The real issue is that the model correctly prevents A from claiming pixels already owned by B — A flows around instead. But during animation, if A ultimately owns territory on the far side of B (having gone around), the final colors make it look like A passed through, when really it just surrounded a thin region. The user might be seeing a large country's front sweep around a small one, creating that visual illusion of passing through. stop at the boundary in the model, but the animation rendering might create a visual artifact where the glow or front-band appears to pass through the smaller region rather than flowing around it — this could be due to how the pixel reveal timing interacts with the coloring and glow effects. The real issue is that the glow band in the animation—which highlights the most recently revealed pixels—gets scattered across all active fronts globally since arrival times interleave between countries, so it doesn't represent a single coherent wavefront but rather a distributed set of pixels that arrived within the same narrow time window.

And checking the mechanics again: when one country's front tries to claim a pixel already owned by another, the union-find check prevents the overwrite, so the front simply flows around the obstacle instead of passing through. The appearance of breakthrough is just the low resolution combined with the color-by-final-owner rendering making it look like one country expanded beyond another after flowing around it. the clearest way forward is to give a straightforward answer grounded in how the algorithm actually works, then offer a concrete demonstration—either a higher-resolution animation or a zoomed view of a specific scenario like a small nation surrounded by a larger one—to make the behavior visually obvious. The "passing through" effect is actually the animation coloring each pixel by its final owner—when A flows around B, both the near and far sides end up A-colored, which can visually read as A going through B even though the fronts properly halt and divert. I'll clarify this distinction and offer to bump up the resolution or show a zoomed frame to make the flow-around behavior unambiguous. On the asset question, I'm considering whether to replace the raster map files with vector formats.

The simulation data is fundamentally raster-based: the choropleth maps show pixelated territory boundaries from the grid itself, so converting to SVG would require vectorizing those jagged edges into clean polygons—a massive undertaking with hundreds of fragments that'd bloat the file size and slow rendering compared to PNG. The ID buffer encodes country identifiers directly in RGB pixel values for click-detection, which is inherently raster and can't be meaningfully converted to vector. The line layers (borders, coast, imposedness) are the only real candidates for vectorization, but there's a fundamental tension: while SVG would render crisply at any zoom level, the underlying simulation data is pixel-based at 0.1° resolution (about 11km), so vectorizing would just smooth the pixelated edges without adding actual detail. The tradeoff isn't worth it—larger files, broken picking mechanisms, and no real information gain. A better path forward would be increasing the raster resolution itself with larger PNGs. a distinct color so the user can visually compare the model's predicted territory against the actual border. I can either trace the boundary dynamically in JavaScript when the toggle is enabled, or use the pre-rendered real borders image if it's efficient enough. I can add a toggle for displaying the real territorial boundary of a selected country in a distinct color like cyan, overlaying it on top of the model's predicted envelope so users can directly compare how well the simulation matches reality. Then there's a more fundamental model change to consider: implementing an enclave annexation rule where if one country's region becomes completely surrounded by another country's territory, it gets absorbed into that surrounding country with population and growth rates recalculated accordingly.

The tricky part is detecting when a region is fully enclosed during the dynamic front propagation—it's a topological problem. I could handle this as a post-processing step after the fronts stabilize: identify each connected component of every country and check if its boundary only touches a single other country (plus ocean), then reassign fully surrounded enclaves to their enclosing neighbor and recompute the population and speed values, which would then feed back into the simulation dynamics.

I'm weighing a few approaches: a static post-hoc reassignment that's simpler but doesn't capture the dynamic feedback, a fully integrated enclosure detection during the simulation which is complex, or an iterative approach where I run the sim, detect enclosed regions, annex them with updated populations, and re-run until it stabilizes. Given the complexity, I should probably present these tradeoffs to the user and implement this as a separate simulation variant rather than baking it into the core logic.

For detecting fully enclosed enclaves in the final partition, I can label each country's connected components, check what other countries or ocean border each component, and if a component only touches one other country, it's enclosed and gets annexed. This cascades as boundaries shift, so I'd iterate until stable. If the user wants population changes to affect growth dynamics, that would require re-running the simulation after each annexation.

I should address all four options conversationally—implement the straightforward ones like the real border toggle, sketch out the enclave annexation as a separate mode so they can compare results, and discuss what 1 and 2 are really asking for versus what would need a full re-simulation. I'll implement the border toggle right away since that's straightforward, then for the separate mode I'll explain the design approach and ask which formulation makes sense—post-hoc enclosure annexation or a dynamic variant—before building it out. country's seed belongs to A initially, but if A's main body never connects to it during growth, that isolated component gets absorbed by B instead. The tricky part is detecting this dynamically during the simulation—when a component of A becomes fully surrounded by B's territory with no unclaimed frontier left, that's when the merger should trigger.

I could implement this in the event-driven sim by tracking each component's open frontier and checking if it closes while surrounded by a single country, then annexing it. It's a moderate implementation effort, so I'm thinking of proposing it as a new simulation variant with its own layer toggle for enclave absorption, though that means generating a parallel set of map assets.

Given the scope, I'll implement the real border toggle now as a clean win, provide a solid design for the enclave absorption feature, and offer to build it separately—either as a post-hoc pass or fully dynamic within the simulation. Хорошие вопросы — разберу каждый честно, и пункт 3 сразу реализую.

1) Проходит ли фронт «сквозь» чужой регион? Нет — это исключено самой моделью, и дело в разрешении + способе раскраски анимации. В событийном алгоритме фронт может занять только незанятую клетку; встретив клетку, уже принадлежащую другой стране, он останавливается и образует границу (слияние происходит лишь между регионами одной страны). То есть A физически обтекает B по периметру. Иллюзию «сквозь» создают две вещи: сетка ~11 км (мелкая страна — несколько пикселей, и обтекание не читается), и то, что анимация красит каждый пиксель его финальным владельцем — когда A обошёл B и замкнулся с другой стороны, дальние пиксели A появляются позже, а так как обе стороны цвета A, это выглядит как «прошёл насквозь». Могу сделать зум-демо конкретного анклава в высоком разрешении, чтобы это наглядно подтвердить.

2) Заменить PNG на SVG? В основном нет, и вот почему. ids_sim/ids_real.png — это пиксельный буфер id страны в каналах RGB, по нему работает определение страны под курсором через getImageData; в SVG такого попиксельного буфера нет. arrival_sim.png — попиксельные времена прихода (16 бит) для анимации, тоже сугубо растровые. Заливки (map_*) получены из пиксельной симуляции — векторизация дала бы гигантские рваные полигоны (970+ осколков), файлы раздулись бы в разы и тормозили. Реальные кандидаты в SVG — только линии (берег, границы), но они тоже трассируются из сетки 11 км, т.е. будут «лесенкой». Линии навязанности у нас уже векторные (JSON→canvas, чёткие на любом зуме). Если цель — резкость при сильном увеличении, дешевле поднять разрешение растров или векторизовать только береговую/национальную обводку. Скажете — сделаю что-то из этого.

3) Реальная граница выбранной страны — делаю сейчас (отдельный тумблер, рисую контур реальной территории страны поверх, для сравнения с моделью/огибающей).

4) Режим поглощения анклавов — ниже, после реализации п.3.

Теперь по пункту 4 — режим поглощения анклавов. Идея отличная и логично достраивает модель, но это уже изменение самой симуляции, поэтому есть развилки — опишу, как вижу, и соберу по вашему слову (как отдельный слой-вариант, чтобы сравнивать с базовым).

Правило: связная компонента страны A, чья вся сухопутная граница примыкает ровно к одной другой стране B, переходит к B; население A-компоненты вливается в связную область B, скорость её фронта пересчитывается (∝√нового населения).

Две реализации:

Динамическая (буквально по вашей формулировке) — ловить замыкание прямо в ходе распространения: как только открытый фронт компоненты исчерпан и весь её периметр оказался против одной B, сливаем в B (с бампом версии/скорости, ускоряя весь фронт B). Точнее всего отражает «пересчёт скорости по ходу», но детектор замыкания внутри событийного алгоритма сложен и его легко сделать с ошибкой.

Итеративная (рекомендую) — прогон базовой модели → находим замкнутые компоненты → аннексируем → перезапуск симуляции с населением анклава, зачтённым B → повторяем до стабилизации. Даёт тот же пересчёт населения и скорости (через повторный прогон), но проще и надёжнее в проверке; каскады (освобождение одних анклавов порождает другие) сходятся за несколько итераций.

Один вопрос по определению, он меняет результат: считаем ли касание океана разрывающим окружение? Моё предложение — да: прибрежный эксклав (выходит к морю) не «окружён страной», поэтому не поглощается; поглощаются только полностью сухопутные анклавы (типа Лесото внутри ЮАР, Сан-Марино внутри Италии, Калининград если он со всех сторон сухопутно зажат). Если хотите — могу, наоборот, считать океан «нейтральной» границей и поглощать и приморские.

Если согласны с итеративным вариантом и «океан разрывает окружение» — соберу это как отдельный переключаемый слой «с поглощением анклавов» (своя карта, id-буфер, площади, рейтинги), с проверкой в браузере. Или, если предпочитаете честно динамический детектор внутри алгоритма — сделаю его, просто это дольше и потребует аккуратного тестирования на синтетических случаях.
